In summary, our research is concerned with
how nutrients are transported and how their concentrations are regulated in brain.
the molecular biology of nutrient transport systems in the central nervous system, and how this information is being applied to the understanding and treatment of neurologic diseases.
understanding how nutrient homeostatic mechanisms work in normal brain, and how they are disrupted in neurologic disorders.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
‘we are just now beginning to learn how the brain is fed and how nutrient homeo-stasis in brain and CSF is achieved’.

the brain is a very special organ that requires special transporters for the uptake of nutrients, and that the transporters have evolved to provide for the unique metabolic and physiologic requirements of brain.
the brain and CSF transport systems for these nutrients are highly efficient, specific, and regulated in a coordinated manner to maintain the appropriate levels of these essential nutrients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ‘why’ and ‘how’ are known for most of the nutrient transport systems in brain and CSF.
‘neurochemistry’ has become ‘neurogenetics’.
we are now at a point where we can predict that a patient with a given genetic defect (e.g., MTHFR) will respond to a given treatment (e.g., high folate intake).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain and CSF have a high level of metabolic and neurochemical autonomy, and are not merely ‘passive recipients’ of blood and CSF nutrients.

, for each crucial nutrient (glucose, folates, and ascorbic acid), there are multiple transport systems, and that the systems that transport the crucial nutrient into CSF are distinct from those that transport it across the blood– brain barrier.

the brain is not just a ‘special organ’ but a unique one that has evolved to require a unique combination of nutrients, and has developed unique mechanisms to transport and maintain these nutrients in a highly regulated manner.
